Text: {{c1::Therapeutic communication::technique}} uses both {{c2::verbal and nonverbal}} techniques to {{c3::encourage patients to express how they feel and to build a positive relationship}}.
Back Extra:
Why: nonverbal cues (posture, facial expression, eye contact) carry as much of the message as the spoken words do.

Cue: the aim is a positive, trusting relationship, not just gathering facts.

Text: The tone, pace, and volume of a patient's speech reveal the person's {{c1::mood}} and the perceived {{c2::importance}} of the message.
Back Extra:
Ex: a patient yelling that his chest is killing him may be angry, scared, or both, on top of being in pain.

Pitfall: listen to how something is said, not only the words, or you miss half the message.

Text: Direct eye contact conveys {{c1::honesty and respect}} in the United States and most European countries, but conveys {{c1::confrontation}} in Latin American, Asian, and African cultures.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: a North American EMT may wrongly read a patient who looks away as hiding something or untrustworthy, when the patient is simply being polite by their own culture.

Why: people tend to interpret messages through their own worldview.

Text: {{c1::Ethnocentrism::bias}} is {{c2::considering your own cultural values as more important when interacting with people of a different culture}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: ethnocentrism is privately judging your own culture as superior; cultural imposition goes further and actively forces those values onto the patient.

Pitfall: it quietly skews your read of a patient, e.g. assuming someone who avoids eye contact is being deceptive.

Text: {{c1::Cultural imposition::bias}} is {{c2::forcing your own cultural values onto a patient because you believe your values are better}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: cultural imposition is the extreme of ethnocentrism, ethnocentrism only ranks your culture higher, cultural imposition acts on it against the patient.

Ex: a physician angrily accusing parents of abuse over the harmless Asian healing practice of coining is cultural imposition.

Text: Your patient is Thai and has a bleeding scalp wound, but in Thai culture the head is deeply personal and touched only by intimates. What should you do before treating the head? {{c1::Ask permission first, if at all possible}}
Back Extra:
Why: all aspects of communication, including touch, have a cultural foundation, so respecting it builds trust even during care.

Pitfall: recognize and respect a patient's culture even during a life-threatening emergency, not only when it is convenient.

Text: In communication, {{c1::noise::obstacle}} is {{c2::anything that dampens or obscures the true meaning of a message}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: literal noise is sounds in the environment; lighting, distance, and physical obstacles are other physical factors that obscure the message.

Distinguish: this is physical/literal noise, a barrier to the message, not the message's actual content.
